\smallskip\noindent\textbf{2.1 Phonology} We will rely on
fully formed \textit{words} as well as their atomic components,
\textit{morphemes}, as our basic signs, and we assume, without argumentation,
the usual computational theory of phonetics/phonology/morpho\-phonology and
morphology that has proven capable of handling these. As is well known, purely
segmental phonological representations are efficiently handled by finite state
transducers (FSTs) \citep{Koskenniemi:1983a}, and the mechanism can be
extended to autosegmental representations
\citep{Goldsmith:1976,Goldsmith:1990,Kornai:1995}.

Since we will have many occasions to use finite state mechanisms, we repeat
here the classic definition \citep{Moore:1956} whereby a \textbf{finite
  automaton} $\mathcal{A}$ is given as a 6-tuple $\langle S,i, \Sigma, O,
\delta, G\rangle$ where $S$ is the set of \textit{states} with a distinguished
$i\in S$ \textit{initial state}, $\Sigma$ and $O$ are the \textit{input and
  output alphabets} respectively. The machine, upon receiving input $a \in
\Sigma$ in some state $s \in S$, transitions according to the
\textit{transition function} $\delta: S\times\Sigma \rightarrow 2^S$, and
outputs a signal $\alpha$ according to the \textit{output function} $G: S
\rightarrow O^*$.

The original Moore definition is slightly generalized by permitting
nondeterministic transitions (codomain of $\delta$ is $2^S$ rather than just
$S$) and arbitrary strings as signals (codomain of $G$ is $O^*$ rather than
just $O$), but the main definitional novelty will come in Section~\ref{onto}
because we will have reasons to permit the storage of finitely many (positive,
time-dependent) predicates $p$ that serve as the instantaneous description of
the state. Also, for modeling communication we will consider finite
\textit{networks} of finite automata that can send/receive signals, but this
does not add any generality, the resulting compound systems are still finite
state.

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{2.2 Syntax} The syntax mechanism we envision is not very
different: for local patterns we assume \textit{constructions}
\citep{Fillmore:1997} akin to the \textit{tagmemes} of \cite{Pike:1967}, and
for long-distance effects we will use \texttt{=agt} and \texttt{=pat} as
\textit{linkers}. \fl uses a theory of linking (or slot-filling) that has its
origins in work of P\={a}\d{n}ini's theory of \textit{k\={a}rakas}
\citep{Ostler:1979,Kiparsky:1987,Butt:2006}, see VS2.4.  There is no need to increase the
formal power of the finite state system defined above, because linking could
be handled by the same autosegmental mechanism that is used in phonology
\citep{Sadock:1985}. We stand neutral on the debate whether linkers are best
seen as grammatical functions \citep{Bresnan:1983}, as deep cases
\citep{Fillmore:1968}, or as thematic (proto)roles \citep{Dowty:1989}, the
salient point is that \fl has \textit{only} these two, in particular there are
no `3' (indirect object) or other linkers at any level of the description.

The fact that LLMs are clearly capable of natural language parsing and
generation provides strong empirical evidence in favor of the view that finite
state mechanisms are sufficient for linguistic competence.  We emphasize that
word vectors, initially seen as having continuous coordinates, have also been
quantized without significant performance loss
\citep{Zafir:2019,Cohn:2023,Talamadupula:2024}, so treating LLMs as giant FSTs
is fully justified, and their use in no way calls for an increase in the
formal power of the system.

will make heavy use of the \fl formalism, which relies on the unification of
nodes in the tradition of \cite{Shieber:1986,Hellwig:2003}, but for the most

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{2.4 Pragmatics} Phenomena such as presupposition or
implicature are often subsumed under a separate heading of pragmatics.
\citep{Gazdar:1979} takes the hardline position that the proper domain of
pragmatics is defined by complementarity to the better-understood domain of
semantics: those, and only those, semanto-pragmatic phenomena belong there
that cannot receive a proper explanation in terms of model-theoretic
semantics. Here we accept this hardline position, but with an important
caveat: we take the `pragmatic wastebasket' to be empty, i.e. we argue that
\textit{all} such phenomena can already receive a semantic explanation. We
argue that neither presuppositions nor implicature (nor any other phenomenon
generally discussed under this heading) require any extension of the semantic
mechanism discussed here, the finite state machinery of \fl is already
sufficient \citep{Kornai:2018b}. 

In summary, the \textit{material} of causation are the ideas, modeled by the
formulas themselves: ideas cause other ideas, in a way that is not any
different from physical events/situations causing other other physical
events/situations. In fact, we have no use for a separate `mental' realm as
distinct from the ordinary `physical' realm.

\subsection{Causal systems}

the main task of this section is to translate between the
automata-theoretic view of intent sketched in Section~1 above and the
structural equations used in Sections~2-3 of FH. This is made easier by
automata being close to the \cite{Halpern:2016} causality setup. The notion of
causalty presented in \cite{Kornai:2024a} divides the concept in two parts:
{\tt x ECause y} is simply temporal succession, {\it post hoc Ergo propter
  hoc}, whereas {\tt x SCause y} requires some s such that {\tt x Initiate s}
and {\tt s ECause y}. In other words, it requires intention on x's part to
create a {\it Sine qua non} cause-effect pair.

One difference between the HP definition of causality and the naive \fl
\citep{Kornai:2015a} definition is that we see no reason to exclude the
circular case, and consider it perfectly reasonable to assume that night
causes day, day causes night (see \cite{Kornai:2022} 3.2 for discussion of the
cyclic worldview, and 6.2 for a discussion of the cycle of violence). Another
one is the treatment of probabilities: whereas HP is very friendly to
probabilistic analysis, the naive K system can only do this with a great deal
of effort, and the results are not nearly as good \citep{Gyenis:2019}.

\subsection{Translating from FH to \fl}

Let us first translate FH's causality setup to automata.  {\it Variables} will
be fluents stored at various machine states, in particular {\it exogenous}
variables are stored in affarent neurons. If we restrict FH to the binary
case, {\it structural equations} are just propositional formulas. One could
trivially translate {\it action variables} to efferent neurons, but this is
not quite satisfactory, because we want to take into account purely mental
actions as well. Also, it is clear from FH that the intent is to treat actions
as choices among many possible outcomes, not just binary choices, though one
could always reduce n-way choice to $\log_2 n$-compounded binary choices.

The key issue for us is mental action. This can be a simple commitment to some
future action or outcome, but it may involve the laborious construction of a
plan that leads there, the MBUILD of \cite{Schank:1975}. Such mental activity
is evident when we play chess or just want to pleasantly surprise someone on
their birthday. On FH terms this is a disjunctive goal: she would be
pleasantly surprised from a nice gift but also from hearing an amateur poem we
composed just for the occasion.



\subsection{Translating from \fl to FH}

\fl uses automata {\it states} in two senses: first, as nodes in the transition
graph, and second, as memory locations where information is stored. The
ambiguity between these two usages is mild: if a location can store only one
bit, changing this is the same as minimally (on one coordinate) changing the
state vector that describes the automaton. In fact, the classic neural net
model \citep{McCulloch:1943} does exactly this, the bit `stored' in a neuron
is just its activation level. If we assume (as \fl does) the storage of more
complex entries that require $n$ bits, this is still easy to translate back to
$n$ elementary neurons. The key issue is that some of these entries are
persistent on a multi-year scale, while others are transient (are built up and
dissolved on a subsecond scale).

One mental act that we single out as cardinal is {\it writing} in long-term
memory: when we devise a plan (a deterministic finite automaton) we must
commit it to memory. The other important act is {\it realization,} in a sense
the dual of planning: as we go ahead with putting our plan into practice, at 
each step update the mental pointer (on case of disjunctive plans, set of
pointers) to the current state(s).

Normally, plans are generated by backward chaining: suppose my end-goal is to
surprise someone by an expensive gift. At step $n-1$ I need to buy it, but to
transfer the price to the vendor will require money in my checking account.
Therefore in step $n-2$ I will sell some asset and do a bank-internal transfer
from savings to checking. Step $n-3$ is therefore to log in and check which
asset is best to sell, let's say this is the first step of my plan (so $n$
will be 4). So my plan is a 4-state deterministic automaton, and while
performing some of these acts may only take a few keystrokes, the time it
takes for sales orders to be executed and for money to be transferred may be
on the multi-day scale, and at any stage I need to verify whether the
preconditions of the next step are met or not yet. 

A note on terminology: when we discuss {\it plans} we steer close to the
ordinary sense of this word `a set of actions for achieving something in the
future, especially a set of actions that has been considered carefully and in
detail'. \cite{Schank:1977} use ``plan'' in a technical sense that is closer
to the FH sense of intent, ``connecting the goal state to a set of possible
actions to realize that state'' (p 71), whereas the naive sense of plan we use
is closer to Schankian {\it scripts,} with the main difference that we
consider plans to carry both fulfilment conditions and time constraints at
each stage. Perhaps a better name for FH `intent' and Schankian `plan' would
be {\it tactic} as the term is used in theorem proving \citep{Gauthier:2021}.

\subsection{Tentative mapping}

Returning to FH's structural equations, the range function $\mathcal{R}$ maps
\fl automata on the values they can take i.e. the states they can be in. For a
deterministic automaton D this is simply the set of nodes N in the transition
graph of D, but for a nondeterministic automaton it is some subset of
$2^N$. This definition of range may later be in need of refinement in terms of
the fluents we permit at the nodes. (In theory, such fluents are just
abbreviatory devices that could be completely eliminated from the automata,
but in practice it is very hard to formulate any regularity/rule without the
abbreviatory language, just as it would be hard to study mechanics without
vectors.) 

Now (we are at the top of p 3 in FH) for each internal sub-automaton (FH's
endogeneous variable) X we have a function $F_X$ from a direct product to the
range of $X$, with this product taken over the range of exogenous variables, 
i.e. the set of affarent input possibilities $\times$ the set of all other
internal subautomata (other than $X$, that is) states.

If this is correct, FH envision the entire finite system of variables as a
finite set of automata which are themselves governed by the affarent inputs
and the state(s) of the other automata deterministically. The \fl view differs
mostly in assuming that such governance need not be deterministic, but this
difference is rather easily paved over by permitting the ranges to include
state sets as well.

Taking a page from the standard NDFA implementation method we assume that each
automaton has a set of nodes $N$ (which we conceive of as registers capable of
storing complex data structures themselves) and a set of pointers to these
nodes. Initially, there is only one pointer, pointing at the distinguished
initial state of the automaton, but as inputs are received and pointers are
moved the automaton may transition nondeterministically, in which case we add
a pointer to each state so reached. In an irenic spirit, we will simply say
that $\mathcal{R}$ is composed of state sets, with the deterministic case
(probably the only one intended by FH) corresponding to these sets all being
singletons. 

\subsection{Time}

The above formalism is very broad, any variable can affect any other variable.
In \fl we have small automata corresponding to each lexical entry, so we are
talking about $10^4$ (at least $10^2$, at most $10^6$) variables. We assume a
certain amount of locality in the form of a binary matrix $M$ whose $i,j$-th
element tells us whether the value $X_i$ is taking can, or cannot, affect the
state that $X_j$ has. The more sparse $M$ the stronger the locality. In one
limiting case there are only a few zeros and we obtain the original FH
definition, in the other $M$ is a direct sum of permutation matrices each
corresponding to a (reflex) cycle. Empirical study of the lexicon of human
languages shows a small core, (less than a hundred items in
\cite{Goddard:2002}, less than 800 in the more formal \cite{Kornai:2022}) from
which all other entries are reachable, and a rather sparse structure within
the core, with less than 1\% of the $M$ entries filled.

Given the foregoing we may see the FH and \fl approaches as differing only in
the setting of the sparseness parameter, with the rest of the differences
`variables' and `values' on one side, `automata' and `states' on the other,
being more linguistic than substantial. Yet there seems to be an area, {\it
  rhythm generation}, where the FH approach may be wanting, A harmonic
oscillator already requires some notion of a derivative, and a differential
equation (even a discretized version) requires the values and the deltas to
appear in the same equation. 


\section{Nodal decomposition}

Consider a set of {\it nodes} $N_i (i=1,\ldots,k)$. We think of these as
automata, FH think of them as varibles, the terminology is chosen to be
neutral between the two. Each will have {\it activity levels} $a_{ij}
(i=1,\ldots,k; j=1,\ldots,l_i). There are some (directional) {\it channels}
summarized in a connectivity matrix $C_{ij}$, and a finite set of symbols
$\Sigma$ being the union of the channel alphabets $\Sigma_{ij}$ which are
assumed to share a single `blank' symbol 0.

So far, this is very standard, and makes for convenient modeling of all kinds
of computational devices from Petri nets to finite state transducers. 
A somewhat unusual assumption that we will make here is that each node has its
own {\it timescale}. 

\section{Ontology}\label{onto}

The goal of the ontology is to explicate what exists or, in more formal terms,
what can participate in a model structure. In general, contemporary modal
logic \citep{Blackburn:2001} employs the same model-theoretic formalization as
classical predicate calculus, with each model structure given by a base set
$W_i$ of atomic objects and some relations on it that have the same arity for
each $i\in I$.  While there is some (mild) disagreement on whether the indexes
run over possible worlds, situations, or information states, this is often
considered a `metaphysical' detail, assuming simply the existence of some
\textit{points} for evaluating predicates, collected in the index set
$I$. Following \cite{Kripke:1963} a binary accessibility relation $R \subset I
\times I$ is employed in the analysis of unary modal operators, and as argued
in \cite{Beall:2012}, a ternary accessibility relation $T \subset I \times I
\times I$ may be fruitfully used in the analysis of binary modals such as
relevant implication. Here we build out this apparatus only to the extent it
is directly relevant for a formal reconstruction of projection and blending in
mental spaces, as exemplified by blending two rather different notions, ECause
and SCause. 

\smallskip\noindent\textbf{5.3 Automata} are small in the sense that they only
have a handful of functional parts: the state set $S$, the transition function

$R_i$, this means that the input state is constant within the current
$R_{i+1}$ unit, but we also permit finitely many fluents $P_j$ whose value can
change from one $R_i$ unit to the next. A register capable of holding a long
integer has over four billion states, yet it requires only 32 fluents for
describing its current state, and we achieve a similar $2^l$ simplification by
taking the automaton to be the control of a Turing Machine, and permitting a

standard FSTs are capable of transforming the string above the inference line
to the string below, so by combining the right steps in the right order, if
given sufficient tape for holding the entire proof tree, finite state
mechanisms are sufficient for proof checking. (By systematically checking
putative proof candidates of increasing length, they are also capable of
generating proofs, but we will not pursue this matter here.)

To obtain \texttt{SCause}, it is not enough to emphasize the locality
condition already present in \texttt{cause}. Let us revisit 1-13 from 4.1 in

happening before the serpent's eating of them, and superficially meeting the

for the serpent to eat), are clearly not in the \texttt{SCause} relation. This
is because the naive worldview already interpolates a wilful act in the chain
of events: 1a the laying of eggs causes them to be visible to the snake; 1b
the snake seeing them raises the snake's appetite; and 1c following its
appetite is what causes the snake to eat them. In tales, crows can speak, and
snakes could in principle wisely refrain from following their appetites, so
the mere fact of eggs being present only enables their eating but doesn't
quite cause it: for that the volitional step 1c. is also required.

Let us analyze the subchain 1a-c using the apparatus we already built.
Clearly, 1a is enabling, but not \textit{sine qua non}: the snake could become
aware of the existence of eggs by other means than vision, even by speculative
deduction based on the habits of crows. This would, however, entail a
worldview that requires attributing an internal model of its environment to
the snake, and considerable deductive capabilities. Today, we may feel more
comfortable attributing such powers to humans and perhaps higher automata like
LLMs. Whether it is its vision or its heat perception that makes the eggs
visible to the snake is irrelevant: in both cases we require a theory of
object perception whereby objects cause disturbances, the disturbances radiate
outward, and senses are capable of perceiving them. The outward
propagation/radiation of the disturbances is physical necessity, and the
existence of senses capable of perceiving these is a psychophysiological
given, one that we do not hesitate to list as a knowledge postulate.

That coherent disturbances in perceptual qualia lead to object perception is
again something we feel comfortable postulating, as is the object perception
putting a motive force (appetite) in the snake's mind. But even if the snake
is an automaton, the sum of its appetites, so far we do not see
\texttt{SCause} at work, since it may perform the act purely randomly, just as
we, conscious and ethical beings, may crush some bug underfoot without even
knowing about it, and there is no reason to assume that we are doing so by
following some bug-crushing instinct. For humans, both the legal tradition and
common sense requires an act of free will, \textit{intention} to perform the
act, as criterial, \textit{sine qua non}, for culpability. %This is not to say
%that we need to attribute ill will to termites before we fumigate the house:
%we remove them even more easily if we consider them automata.
But for \texttt{SCause} we need not just preponderant force, we also need a
deliberate act. Consider the detective story \textit{A safecracker and an
  arsonist} by \v{C}apek, where a disgruntled apprentice, Sepp, leaves a
magnifying glass, precisely positioned to collect the sunbeams and ignite the
house of his former employer, Anton, on his name-day, June 13th, several
months after he left. This is \textit{sine qua non} causation, obviously
premeditated, and accomplished only by means of having a very good internal
model of the Sun's apparent orbit.\footnote{The moral of the story is
  expressed by the narrator, ``What happened later to this Sepp, I don’t know;
  but I keep thinking how that young hooligan could have been an astronomer
  some day, or a physicist. Why, he could have been a second Newton or
  something, that damned kid!''} The story displays both aspects of
\texttt{SCause} that we identified. The sustained effort is mental, but no
less causative for that: once the plan is set in motion, physical necessity
takes over, making the result inevitable. It is precisely because we see a
significant chain of wilful acts (computing the orbit and positioning the
magnifying glass accordingly) that we consider Sepp culpable.

Note that culpability does not extend to the proximate cause of the fire, the
Sun's rays, since we consider the Sun an automaton. As in other cases, we peg
culpability to the initiator of the automatic action: we say \texttt{a}
\texttt{SCause} \texttt{b} iff \texttt{a} \texttt{Initiate} \texttt{x} such
that \texttt{x} \texttt{cause} \texttt{b}. In the more compact notation
offered by relation composition, \texttt{SCause} = \texttt{Initiate} $\circ$
\texttt{cause}. Any description of what it means to initiate something will
generally involve the assumption that this requires an animate subject with
its own free will. If the grammatical subject is an automaton as in
\textit{the decaying tooth started to hurt} we have two choices: either we
`animate' it (attribute willpower to it, as is commonly done in mythology by
assuming Gods for the sea, the winds, the planets, and other large-scale
automata), or we need to absorb its doings in the \texttt{cause} portion of
the causal chain and trace responsibility further back, to the maker of the
automaton, as far back as Aristotle's unmoved mover if need be.

\medskip\noindent To summarize, the \texttt{SCause} analysis of causation
builds on \texttt{cause} by adding a wilful act at the beginning of the
chain. This succeeds not only in reconstructing Aristotle's motivation for the
\textit{primum movens}, but also sheds light on the nature of mechanical
causation in that \texttt{cause} must be assumed to pertain not just to
ordinary (linear) timelines but to cyclic ones as well. Importantly,
\texttt{SCause} requires a wilful act even for physical/mechanical
causation. Aristotle has conveniently lodged this act in the unmoved mover,
but in subsequent varieties of natural philosophy, every form of automatic
behavior is sustained by God's will, i.e. by physics. This concept is
preserved to this day in legal terminology, which considers natural hazards
outside human control such as earthquakes, mudslides etc. to be ``acts of
God''. Here it is preserved in the very fabric of the model theory, since
rather small automata are already capable of creating large stretches of
time. 

\noindent
On Aristotle's analysis, final cause (telos) also requires some individual $M$
for whom the question `what is it good for' can be answered affirmatively: it
is good for $M$. In particular, voluntary acts that serve no higher goal, such
as collecting pictures of owls, can only be explained by assuming they are
good for the collector, who does this wilfully. Some forms of causation are
blind, proceeding mechanistically, we put these under ECause. Others require a
beneficiary who can set voluntary goals, we put these under SCause. To make
this work requires models that actually contain not just objects subject to
mechanistic law, but also beings capable of complex behavior such as setting
their own goals, so we need to endow the model theory with these. The good
thing is that this requires no extra machinery, the difference between ECause
and SCause boils down to a distinction between deterministic and
nondeterministic automata \citep{Rabin:1959}.

theory of co-presence: for example ice melts because heat (a caloric fluid)
enters it. We will use the relation \texttt{At} to denote \textit{locality},

or any other interaction) to be possible between them.

must be adjacent to the effect. Here we will concentrate on temporal locality.

We begin with the analysis of the naive theory of causation, often stated
as \textit{post hoc ergo propter hoc}. As is well known, this only addresses
a necessary but insufficient condition of causation, but this already requires 
some kind of \textit{implicit serialization}, that only one event can
take place in a single instant. If there are several forces, they need to
appear sequentially. If there is a single timeline, the analysis is quite
reasonable, and works well with iterated causality. 

% and how they can replace the causal models
                           % of \citet{Halpern:2005} in the hereditarily


Altogether, our analysis of causation rests on `happening after', with two
significant changes to standard temporal logic, the use of multiple scales and
a more permissive treatment of discontinuous fluents. It requires some force
to change a fluent: we say that $x$ \texttt{cause} $y$ requires there to be a
time instance $z$ when forces are present, and a change of state from $x=\neg
y$ to $y$ with $x \leq z \leq y$. We are somewhat cavalier here about
identifying the force with the time instance \texttt{z} and about the
important distinction between $<$ and $\leq$, but for the purposes of this
discussion these don't make any difference.

It is the force requirement that makes the ordinary transitivity inference
fail: even if \texttt{a} \texttt{cause} \texttt{b} and \texttt{b}
\texttt{cause} \texttt{c}, it does not necessarily follow that \texttt{a}
\texttt{cause} \texttt{c}, since between \texttt{a} and \texttt{c} we don't
necessarily find a single intervening world \texttt{b} where forces are present
to cause turning \texttt{a} into \texttt{c}. Rather, we have \textit{two}
intervening worlds, one containing the forces whereby \texttt{a} can turn into
\texttt{b}, and the other containing those forces that turn \texttt{b} into
\texttt{c}.  Given the serialization requirement we imposed above, there is no
guarantee that these forces are co-present in the same unit at one faster
scale, so chains of causation such as exhibited in (1-12) have decreasing
implicational power the longer they get. At any point, things could go wrong:
Jackal may not be a true friend of Crow and may provide a pointless plan, the
servants may not be able to keep up with the flight of Crow and thus not find
the burrow, etc. The only situation where a causative step is really and truly
binding is one where the law that it exploits is not just lexical (since
lexical rules are generic, embodying defaults, see \cite{Kornai:2022a} for
discussion) but mechanical, endowed with physical necessity. 
Only the passing of time has this inevitability: the
automata we consider can be nondeterministic/endowed with free will 
\citep{Floyd:1967}, in which case causation also requires \textit{intention}.

Since mechanical causation is by contact (an assumption we will keep in place
for mental causation as well), it follows that the cause and the effect must,
at least for one minim, be co-present in some world.\footnote{Much later,
Leibniz will make do without this assumption, but only at the price of
assuming universal harmony.}





$f_{\sigma}$, and assign a separate location `square' $s_i$ to each cell on
the tape ($1 \leq i \leq l$). If we add a constraint of exclusion, that
$f_{\sigma}$ and $f_{\rho}$ cannot hold in any location at the same time for
$\sigma \neq \rho$ (non-whitespace, non-control) elements, we obtain a large
automaton of $n^l$ states, with each state corresponding to a partially or
fully filled tape. We will use another fluent $a$ to single out the
\textit{active} location where the read-write head resides, so the total
number of states of $T$ is $n^{l+1}$. Reading does not require a separate
operation, in that states of Moore machines can simply broadcast the current
letter under scan, and we use this mechanism to communicate the output from
every movement of the head. Remarkably, the machine requires only $C_2$ time:
each of the operations need to specify the preconditions in the
\texttt{before} state and the resulting configuration in the \texttt{after}
state. As with all systems that operate by law-like regularity, the automaton
always starts in the rest temporal state, which comprises $n^{l+1}$
configuration states (depending on the contents of the tape being simulated
and the position of the read/write head), transitions to the after state, and
gets silently reset to the rest state simply by the passing of time.

We call attention to the fact that the state space of $T$ is only indirectly
related to the tape configurations. The machine itself has no `squares' as
such, the contents of squares are only found by projecting the actual state
space to appropriately chosen coordinates and inspecting the fluents, and
conversely, the entire state space is the direct product of as many simple
automata as we have symbols in $\Sigma \setminus \{\mu,\nu\}$.  This calls for
vectorial notation: at any given time instance, the state vector of $T$ is
given as vector of dimension $l$ containing on the $i$th coordinate the unique
fluent that obtains there. It is these coordinates that act as `squares', but
there is no guarantee that an arbitrary Moore machine can be transparently
decomposed this way.% -- finding a direct product decomposition is part of the
%mapping challenge we will turn to in Section~\ref{map}. 









In the case of $T$, the wire can transmit not just `content' symbols that get
written to the tape, but also `control' symbols which will be reflected only
in the position of the head. (Some readers may find the comparison to the
first 32 `nonprinting' ASCII codes helpful.)

title: GENPLUGIN: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Long-Tail Generative Recommendation with Exposure Bias Mitigation
summary:
Generative recommendation (GenRec) offers LLM integration, reduced embedding
costs, and eliminates per-candidate scoring, attracting great attention.
Despite its promising performance, this study reveals that it suffers from
generation exposure bias and poor long-tail item generalization, two critical
limitations overlooked by prior works on GenRec. To address these, we propose
GENPLUGIN, a plug-and-play framework featuring a dual-encoder, shared-decoder
architecture. During pre-training, it aligns language and ID views via
contrastive learning, harmonizing item representations across two complementary
views. Besides, GENPLUGIN uses a novel training strategy that probabilistically
substitutes ground-truth item ID tokens with predictions from the
language-semantics encoder, alleviating exposure bias. To improve long-tail
generative recommendation, we propose a retrieval-based data augmentation
mechanism. It fine-tunes the decoder of GENPLUGIN to endow GENPLUGIN with the
ability to use relevant users w.r.t. contexts or collaborative information to
augment the generation of item ID tokens in long-tail recommendation scenarios.
We have plugged GENPLUGIN into several representative GenRec models and the
extensive experiments demonstrate that GENPLUGIN can notably mitigate
generation exposure bias during item ID generation while significantly
improving the quality of long-tail item recommendation.

title: Autonomous Computer Vision Development with Agentic AI
summary:
Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems leveraging Large Language Models
(LLMs) exhibit significant potential for complex reasoning, planning, and tool
utilization. We demonstrate that a specialized computer vision system can be
built autonomously from a natural language prompt using Agentic AI methods.
This involved extending SimpleMind (SM), an open-source Cognitive AI
environment with configurable tools for medical image analysis, with an
LLM-based agent, implemented using OpenManus, to automate the planning (tool
configuration) for a particular computer vision task. We provide a
proof-of-concept demonstration that an agentic system can interpret a computer
vision task prompt, plan a corresponding SimpleMind workflow by decomposing the
task and configuring appropriate tools. From the user input prompt, "provide sm
(SimpleMind) config for lungs, heart, and ribs segmentation for cxr (chest
x-ray)"), the agent LLM was able to generate the plan (tool configuration file
in YAML format), and execute SM-Learn (training) and SM-Think (inference)
scripts autonomously. The computer vision agent automatically configured,
trained, and tested itself on 50 chest x-ray images, achieving mean dice scores
of 0.96, 0.82, 0.83, for lungs, heart, and ribs, respectively. This work shows
the potential for autonomous planning and tool configuration that has
traditionally been performed by a data scientist in the development of computer
vision applications.

title: Finding Common Ground: Using Large Language Models to Detect Agreement in Multi-Agent Decision Conferences
summary:
Decision conferences are structured, collaborative meetings that bring
together experts from various fields to address complex issues and reach a
consensus on recommendations for future actions or policies. These conferences
often rely on facilitated discussions to ensure productive dialogue and
collective agreement. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown
significant promise in simulating real-world scenarios, particularly through
collaborative multi-agent systems that mimic group interactions. In this work,
we present a novel LLM-based multi-agent system designed to simulate decision
conferences, specifically focusing on detecting agreement among the participant
agents. To achieve this, we evaluate six distinct LLMs on two tasks: stance
detection, which identifies the position an agent takes on a given issue, and
stance polarity detection, which identifies the sentiment as positive,
negative, or neutral. These models are further assessed within the multi-agent
system to determine their effectiveness in complex simulations. Our results
indicate that LLMs can reliably detect agreement even in dynamic and nuanced
debates. Incorporating an agreement-detection agent within the system can also
improve the efficiency of group debates and enhance the overall quality and
coherence of deliberations, making them comparable to real-world decision
conferences regarding outcome and decision-making. These findings demonstrate
the potential for LLM-based multi-agent systems to simulate group
decision-making processes. They also highlight that such systems could be
instrumental in supporting decision-making with expert elicitation workshops
across various domains.

\abstract{Decision conferences are structured, collaborative meetings that bring together experts from various fields to address complex issues and reach a consensus on recommendations for future actions or policies. These conferences often rely on facilitated discussions to ensure productive dialogue and collective agreement. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown significant promise in simulating real-world scenarios, particularly through collaborative multi-agent systems that mimic group interactions. In this work, we present a novel LLM-based multi-agent system designed to simulate decision conferences, specifically focusing on detecting agreement among the participant agents. To achieve this, we evaluate six distinct LLMs on two tasks: stance detection, which identifies the position an agent takes on a given issue, and stance polarity detection, which identifies the sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral. These models are further assessed within the multi-agent system to determine their effectiveness in complex simulations. Our results indicate that LLMs can reliably detect agreement even in dynamic and nuanced debates. Incorporating an agreement-detection agent within the system can also improve the efficiency of group debates and enhance the overall quality and coherence of deliberations, making them comparable to real-world decision conferences regarding outcome and decision-making. These findings demonstrate the potential for LLM-based multi-agent systems to simulate group decision-making processes. They also highlight that such systems could be instrumental in supporting decision-making with expert elicitation workshops across various domains.}
